locator: §4.1, Geach's example, 'if the entire meaning of ‘tormenting the cat is bad’ in the second premise is well explained by saying that it is suited for use in expressing disapproval'
interpretation: Occasion reading of 'the simplest story of the meaning of moral terms, that they are devices for expressing pro and con attitudes' (emotivism, §2.1: Ayer, Stevenson): the meaning of a moral sentence in an occurrence is exhausted by the attitude it expresses there, which is why, on Geach's argument, it 'cannot be the same' where the sentence is embedded and expresses no disapproval. Only 'same meaning, same expressed attitudes' is formalized. The other defensible reading, that the meaning is the attitude the sentence is suited to express whatever the occurrence, is the expressivists' (SEP-MORAL-COGNITIVISM-2-4-EXPRESSIVIST-MEANING-INVARIANT), recorded as a separate statement. O'Connor's emotivism (OCONNOR-DESTINY-ETHICS-EMOTIVISM) states only the lack of truth value, so whether he holds this reading is not claimed. Attribution reading on a secondary witness: the claim records the position the entry reports, not a thesis of the entry's author. No primary text is pinnable (in copyright, no immutable open text).
